analysis.one_liner: Expands government health coverage for low-income children and adds Medicare benefits, funded by tobacco taxes and reduced overpayments to private Medicare plans.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 225-204 on August 1, 2007, but after the Senate received it in September it sat on the calendar and never came to a vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill renews and expands the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and Medicaid, with the stated goal of enrolling all six million uninsured children who already qualify but are not signed up [S3]. It adds Medicare benefits for seniors — free preventive services, mental health payment parity, and simpler enrollment help for low-income beneficiaries — while cutting payments to private Medicare Advantage plans that exceed the cost of traditional Medicare and raising the minimum rebate drug makers owe Medicaid [S3]. To pay for it, the bill raises federal tobacco taxes [S3]. The House passed it on a mostly party-line vote; the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured children and pregnant women, legal immigrant children, low-income seniors who struggle with Medicare drug-plan costs, and Medicare beneficiaries who would get preventive services without copays. States facing CHIP funding shortfalls also gain more reliable funding.

how_it_helps.text: Title I aims to provide stable CHIP and Medicaid funding to enroll all six million uninsured children who are eligible but not enrolled [S3].

The bill requires CHIP to cover dental care, community health center services, and rural clinic services, adds a 30-day grace period before coverage can be dropped for missed premiums, and lets states cover children up to age 21, legal immigrant children and pregnant women, with 12-month continuous eligibility for children below 200% of poverty [S3].
Medicare beneficiaries get preventive services with no coinsurance or deductible, colorectal cancer screening without a deductible, and equal coinsurance for outpatient mental health care [S3].

Low-income Medicare beneficiaries get easier drug-subsidy enrollment through self-certification and automatic re-enrollment, higher asset limits, an annual out-of-pocket cap, and an end to estate recovery of Medicare cost-sharing assistance for people 55 and older [S3].
Medicare pays private Medicare Advantage plans no more than 100% of what traditional Medicare costs in each county, phased in over four years, ending payments above the traditional rate [S3].
Private Medicare plans face stricter marketing rules, an 85% minimum share of revenue that must go to patient care, and audits that can recover overpayments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Smokers and tobacco companies pay through higher federal excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, and smokeless tobacco; private Medicare Advantage insurers lose excess payments; brand-name drug makers pay larger Medicaid rebates; hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, and imaging providers absorb slightly lower payment updates.

drawbacks.text: The bill is funded by higher tobacco excise taxes, which fall hardest on low-income smokers, though it includes a $500 credit against the increase [S3].

Payment cuts to providers are real: Medicare Advantage plans are phased down to 100% of traditional Medicare costs, the skilled nursing facility update for 2008 is eliminated, home health gets no 2008 inflation update, and hospitals take updates 0.25 points below inflation [S3].

The bill restricts federal CHIP funds for covering adults through waivers unless the state first ensures no eligible child would be denied coverage, and it stops new health opportunity account demonstrations [S3].
Cutting Medicare Advantage payments risked plans reducing benefits or exiting markets, which is why the industry and most Republicans opposed the bill [S9].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect is a large expansion of health coverage for low-income children and better Medicare benefits for low-income seniors, paid for by tobacco taxes and by trimming payments that private Medicare plans and drug makers receive above traditional rates. The main honest objections are that tobacco taxes are regressive and that provider payment cuts could affect access in some markets. On balance the benefits to ordinary people are large and the costs are concentrated on industries receiving above-market payments.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 225-204 on August 1, 2007, but once the Senate received it in September it went on the calendar and never came up for a vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 24, 2007, and referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees; Ways and Means ordered it reported on a 24-17 vote [S7].
The House Rules Committee set a two-hour debate and barred floor amendments, and a Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions failed 202-226 [S7].
On August 1, 2007 the House passed the bill 225-204, with 220 of 231 Democrats voting yes and only 5 of 202 Republicans voting yes [S9].
The Senate received the bill on September 4, 2007, read it twice, and placed it on the legislative calendar, where it remained without a vote through the end of the 110th Congress [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private Medicare Advantage insurers kept the above-traditional-Medicare payments the bill would have phased out, drug makers avoided the higher Medicaid rebate, and tobacco companies faced no tax increase. The six million uninsured children who were already eligible for CHIP remained without coverage.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private Medicare plans and drug makers

for.name: John D. Dingell
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MI), Chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which expanded CHIP, Medicaid, and Medicare protections [S1].

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over CHIP and Medicare (Chair: Charles Rangel, D-NY)
for.what_they_did: Held markup, voted 24-17 to order the bill reported amended, and reported it to the House [S7].

against.name: Kay Granger
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to amend the CHIP title; the motion failed 202-226 [S7].

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought H.R. 3162 to the Senate floor after it was placed on the calendar; the chamber instead pursued a separate bipartisan CHIP compromise through the Finance Committee.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the scale of the CHIP expansion and vetoed the companion SCHIP reauthorization bill that fall, eliminating the realistic path for the House version.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 220 of 231 Democrats voted yes versus only 5 of 202 Republicans, and the failed motion to recommit showed the same split (222 Democrats and 194 Republicans opposed it) [S8].

industries.note: The bill phases their payments down to no more than what traditional Medicare costs in each county, requires an 85% medical loss ratio, tightens marketing rules, and expands audit recovery. Their excess payments came at taxpayer cost without clearly better care, so their interest in blocking the bill ran against both taxpayers and beneficiaries [S3].

The bill raises the minimum Medicaid rebate from 15.1% to 22.1% and broadens the 'best price' definition to include discounts given to pharmacy benefit managers, costing manufacturers revenue that would have come from public drug spending [S4].

Higher excise taxes on cigarettes, cigars, and smokeless tobacco fund the coverage expansion and are intended to reduce smoking; the industry's interest in avoiding the tax conflicts with the bill's public-health purpose [S3].

Hospitals take inflation updates cut by 0.25 points and a moratorium on new long-term care hospitals, but they gain higher disproportionate-share payments for treating the poor and, in some states, newly insured patients through CHIP and Medicaid expansions [S3].

A per-capita fee on health insurance policies and self-insured plans funds the new comparative effectiveness research center; the research it pays for could benefit the system broadly, but the fee is a direct cost to the industry [S4].

The bill cuts imaging payments (75% presumed utilization, a 50% discount on multi-procedure scans, accreditation requirements, no global billing) and starts reforms of misvalued physician services; it also adds new coverage for mental health therapists, nurse-midwives, and medical homes that create new billing opportunities [S3].
